title: Search for the low-mass isotropic signature of QCD instantons in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using the ATLAS detector
comment: 33 pages in total, author list staring page 16, 4 figures, submitted to PRL. All figures including auxiliary figures are available at https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PAPERS/STDM-2021-01/
summary: This Letter presents the first search for QCD instanton-induced events at the LHC. Instantons are semi-classical solutions of the Yang-Mills equations of QCD and correspond to non-perturbative tunneling between topologically distinct vacuum sectors. The search is performed in 1.6 $\text{nb}^{-1}$ of very low instantaneous luminosity proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at 13 TeV. Angular variables based on reconstructed charged-particle tracks are used to discriminate the expected rest-frame isotropy of low-mass instanton events from the minimum-bias background. The minimum-bias event background is predicted using a data-driven technique and reweighted Monte Carlo models. A profile-likelihood fit is performed in a two-dimensional classifier variable to extract a possible signal contribution, yielding an excess of low-mass isotropic events with an observed significance of $3.5σ$.

title: AI-Assisted Analysis of CMS Open Data: Prompt J/psi Cross-Section Measurements in pp and Peripheral PbPb Collisions at sqrt(S)= 7 TeV and sqrt(sNN) = 2.76 TeV
summary: We investigate the use of an artificial-intelligence (AI) coding agent, supervised by human physicists, for collider physics analyses using CMS Open Data. OpenAI Codex performs dimuon event selection, two-dimensional invariant-mass and decay-length fits, Monte Carlo detector simulations, and systematic uncertainty evaluation after acquiring physics and experimental knowledge from published studies and external references, with human review at each stage. The workflow is tested on two CMS datasets, with custom full-detector simulations used to determine acceptance and reconstruction efficiencies. In proton-proton collisions at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV, prompt J/psi differential cross sections are measured versus transverse momentum and rapidity. The ratios of remeasured to published CMS cross sections have a mean of 1.000 and an RMS spread of 0.215 across 39 bins. In peripheral (50-100% centrality) PbPb collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV, the corresponding prompt J/psi fiducial cross-section ratios have a mean of 1.158 and an RMS spread of 0.225 across six intervals. We identify agent failure modes and demonstrate the importance of structured human review in ensuring reliable results.

title: Impact of errors-on-errors on the PDF determination from combined HERA data
summary: We study how the determination of parton distribution functions (PDFs) from the combined HERA inclusive deep-inelastic-scattering data is affected when the quoted sizes of the systematic errors are themselves treated as uncertain. We refer to these uncertainties informally as errors-on-errors and account for them using the Gamma Variance Model, which treats the squared quoted systematic errors as Gamma-distributed estimates of unknown variances. As a result, the usual quadratic nuisance parameter constraints in the $χ^2$ are replaced with logarithmic ones. We present two applications of the framework. In the first, a robustness test estimates the largest errors-on-errors effects that could be present in our reproduction of the HERAPDF2.0 NNLO fit, reducing $χ^2/n_{\rm dof}$ from 1363/1131 to 1306/1131, with the main impact concentrated at low Bjorken $x$ and low squared momentum transfer, $Q^2$. Comparable reductions are observed with a more flexible small-$x$ parametrisation, both at fixed NNLO and with NNLO+NLL$_x$ resummation. In the second, the error-on-error parameters are instead assigned a priori, as they would be in a PDF determination intended for publication. Taken together, the results indicate that errors-on-errors can account for a substantial part of the apparent data-theory tension in the combined HERA dataset, improving the inferred compatibility and widening the fitted PDF uncertainties without appreciably displacing the PDFs or cross-section predictions themselves.

authors: U. De Freitas Carneiro Da Graca
title: Absolute luminosity calibration of the LHCb detector in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with beam-gas imaging
comment: All figures and tables, along with any supplementary material and additional information, are available at https://lhcb-glance.cern.ch/alcm/public/analysis/full-details/4435 (LHCb public pages)
summary: An absolute calibration of the luminosity for proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with the LHCb detector in Run 2 of the LHC is presented. The calibration cross-section of the Vertex counter, a statistic based on reconstructed primary vertices, is measured using the beam-gas imaging method to be $σ_\mathrm{Vertex} = 57.61 \pm 0.06\ (stat) \pm 0.52\ (syst)$ mb, corresponding to a relative precision of 0.91%. This result provides around a factor of two improvement in the precision of the LHCb luminosity calibration used in previous cross-section measurements with this dataset. The largest systematic uncertainties arise from the imperfect knowledge of the beam-gas vertex resolution, the observed fill-by-fill spread of the cross-section, and the choice of transverse beam-profile fit model.

title: Remark on internal relaxation in large number qubit systems
summary: For a time $t_{c}$ of calculation in an $N$ qubit quantum computer that is much shorter than the intrinsic Heisenberg time $t_H$, $t_c\ll t_H$, the dynamics of the system is effectively irreversible and the couplings between the qubits give rise to a relaxation time scale $τ_r$. If $t_H\gg t_c >\sim τ_r$ one looses quantum coherence exponentially fast. Since $t_H$ scales exponentially with $N$ there is a threshold $N_c$ such that for $N\gg N_c$ one must be aware of possible intrinsic relaxation during calculation. As an order of magnitude estimation we find $N_c\approx \ln(τ_r/T)$ where $T$ is a typical system specific oscillation time of a single qubit. $τ_r$ can be estimated as the typical inverse transition rate between two parts of the system, one of which is treated as an environment of the other.

title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
summary: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.

title: CSS circuits are ICM circuits without magic states
summary: Gidney and Jones recently introduced ``CSS circuits'', generated by $X$, $Z$, $\MX$, $\MZ$ and CNOT, and showed that they can be sampled with $O(1)$ work per gate. They suspected that the class had been seen before. We point out that it is, up to a normal form, the initialisation--CNOT--measurement (ICM) form introduced in 2015 for compiling fault-tolerant circuits, restricted to $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{+}$ initialisations. The ICM construction answers constructively their question about ``non-CSS-ness as a resource'': every Clifford$+T$ circuit compiles to a CSS circuit acting on $\ket{Y}$ and $\ket{A}$ input states.

title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout
comment: 26 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables. Models, data and tutorials: https://lfl-lab.github.io/SQuADDS/qcap/
summary: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.

title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code available at https://github.com/yeon-lee/QEDist
summary: We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff $W$, a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most $W$ or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the $[[144,12,12]]$ code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
summary: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

title: Black holes as black boxes: a query lower bound on python's lunch decoding
summary: The python's lunch conjecture relates the complexity of bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks to an exponential cost associated with post-selection. We establish a tight query lower bound for this decoding problem in a Haar random oracle model, with a python's lunch circuit that applies Haar random unitary $U$ to a logical input and fixed ancillas, followed by post-selection on $m$ output qubits. Given one copy of the normalized encoded state and coherent oracle access to $U$ and $U^\dagger$, including controlled queries, we prove that recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires $Ω(2^{m/2})$ queries. Together with the state-independent amplitude amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings, this establishes query complexity $Θ(2^{m/2})$ at constant decoding accuracy. We also comment on the decoding cost for other "admissible'" ensembles of unitaries $U$ which give rise to families of approximately isometric holographic maps.

title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
summary: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

title: A Proposal for Quantum Reference Frames in Quantum Field Theory and their Experimental Exploration
summary: We construct quantum reference frames (QRFs) in quantum field theory, using localized modes of a scalar field as frames for its shift symmetry. We import tools from relativistic quantum information to explicitly compute entropies and correlation measures of relational observables, investigating their frame dependence and the new features arising from the field-theoretic character of the system. Unlike QRFs for systems with finitely many degrees of freedom, localized field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed in physically relevant states and generically correlated with the subsystems they describe. These aspects of QRFs for fields affect the properties of relational observables in a subtle way. Furthermore, we put forward a proposal for testing these predictions with existing quantum simulators based on ultracold atoms and quantum fluids, thus connecting QRF physics with analogue gravity platforms.

title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.

title: Restoring quantum neural network trainability through reusable calibration
summary: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) rely on measured quantum observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise can suppress the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning. Here, we develop a structure-preserving error-mitigation framework that improves QNN trainability through reusable calibration of the quantum circuit's effective noise response. By calibrating a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, we construct regularized estimators of local quantum features that remain fixed throughout training. We quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect the recovery of both observables and their derivatives. Numerical simulations demonstrate enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification performance, and an IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under hardware noise. We further demonstrate calibration reuse in a modular QNN comprising 25 independent four-qubit channels, corresponding to 100 qubits in aggregate. Our results establish reusable feature calibration as a practical approach to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated calibration at every training step.

title: Frequency Multiplexing of Purcell-Enhanced Optically Coherent NV Centers
summary: Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is key to scalable quantum networks. Realizing them with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is hindered by the degradation of optical coherence accompanying nanofabrication. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while preserving near-lifetime-limited optical coherence. We observe linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz, enabling the frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhances the optical emission, consistent with Purcell enhancement predicted by finite-element simulations. Additionally, individual cavities can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip. These results combine bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.

title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
summary: Whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect encoded quantum information has remained a central open question since Kitaev introduced topological quantum computation. Passive protection requires stability against both thermal noise at nonzero temperature and generic static Hamiltonian perturbations Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) recently established unperturbed three-dimensional thermal self-correction using a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians. However, they left open whether their construction remains stable against quantum perturbations, even at zero temperature. In this paper, we show that a slight variant of the BDL code family achieves stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as the system size grows. Following BDL, in the absence of perturbation it is thermally stable below a critical temperature, achieving a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath generated by single-site system-bath interactions satisfying detailed balance with bounded coupling rates. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. To prove this zero-temperature stability, we establish local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the usual Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In the companion paper, we combine the tools developed here with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the phase diagram's positive-temperature perturbed interior.

title: Causality, determinism and predictability: Probing nature through classical and quantum eyes
summary: In this article, mainly focussed on students and interested readers, we discuss how the understanding of causality, determinism and predictability is transformed as we move from the classical world view to the quantum description. We first explain how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outline the notion of causality. A paradigm shift occurs within the framework of quantum mechanics where we have to revisit, and even give up, the notions of determinism, predictability and maybe even strict causality. An engrossing and fascinating debate ensues, after the formulation of quantum mechanics among the giants of physics like Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and many others. While some questions have been settled in the last century in favour of quantum world view, there are still many open questions, most important of which is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.

title: Loss-Tolerant Quantum Correlations Between Atomic and Photonic Qubits
summary: Quantum physics forbids cloning of a qubit. Therefore, a qubit is irreversibly lost upon loss of the information carrier. To mitigate this physical loss, it has been proposed to distribute the logical information across an entangled set of physical qubits, some of which can be lost. Previous experiments illustrated this concept, but failed to demonstrate a gain in the information-retrieval efficiency. Here we address this challenge with photons for which the total loss, from generation to detection, is below the loss-tolerance threshold of $50\%$. Using two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, we encode information into the photons of a graph state and observe an efficiency gain for retrieving quantum correlations between the atoms and the photons for single-qubit measurements in the Pauli $X$ and $Z$ bases. Although technical errors reduce the probability to obtain the \textit{correct} result, we achieve average fidelities as high as $\gtrsim\!70\%$ without and $\gtrsim\!75\%$ with error detection, demonstrating entanglement between the atomic and encoded photonic qubits. Lowering the encoding errors is a next natural step toward loss-tolerant photonic quantum-information processing.

title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler
summary: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.

title: Distrustful entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the one of the most explored application of quantum information theory. While practical QKD systems are being deployed around the world, a major issue of these setups are that one has to trust the measurement devices of both parties. On the other hand, the most secure among such schemes are called device-independent (DI) QKD protocols, where no component of the setup is assumed to be trusted. However, due to their high technological demand, their loophole-free version currently remain out of practical reach. Inspired by the real world, we consider the traditional QKD in a distrustful measurement setting, that is, the measurement devices can only be trusted upto some level of confidence, which might still be large but not completely trusted. We then derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate in this scenario. Then considering perfect detectors and source, and the entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) protocol, we show that to obtain secure keys one needs to trust their devices more than 82 %. However, we observe that such a protocol can not be realised with any level of distrust using the realistic detectors and sources at the current technology. Finally, we also consider the BBM protocol with arbitrary dimensional systems and observe that they are more robust to distrust than qubit systems. Consequently, with the same level of distrust, along with same detector and source efficiences, one can get better key rates with high-dimensional systems.

title: Performance analysis of a Rydberg atom THz radiometer concept
summary: THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature. This warrants investigation into alternative THz receivers such as Rydberg atom sensors, which are highly susceptible to electric fields. In particular, the conversion architecture has been demonstrated to coherently transduce thermal radiation. This system offers room-temperature operation and does not necessarily require a local oscillator at the frequency of the input signal. We provide an assessment of the feasibility of such sensors for THz radiometry within the context of Earth observation.

title: AI Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
summary: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

title: Quantum Reference Frames, Locality, and Microcausality in Quantum Field Theory
summary: As a consequence of the relativistic spectrum condition, quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space are never described by projection-valued measures, and in many cases fail a weaker spacetime localisation property known as the norm-$1$ condition. This has several implications for the local and observable structure of quantum field theories described relative to even the best available frame: for a large class of frame states, strict locality is replaced by almost locality, and microcausality by commutators that decay rapidly with increasing separation, corresponding to an effective smearing of the light cone by the localisation density of the frame state. Operations built from finitely many almost local Kraus operators, for example nonselective measurements of relativised local observables, satisfy an approximate no-signalling bound, with a residue attributable to the localisation uncertainty of the frame. Whether causality in its strongest operational form -- non-disturbance under all physically realisable operations -- survives relativisation is left open. An upshot of our finding is that quantum field theories formulated relative to a quantum reference frame cannot rest on the traditional axioms, and some general relational axiomatisation must replace at least some of them by taking into account physically realistic properties of the frame.

title: Transient State Preservation of a Dissipative Qubit via Lyapunov Control
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE URUCON 2026
summary: Preserving quantum states in the presence of environmental decoherence remains a fundamental challenge for quantum information processing. This work investigates whether Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback can transiently preserve the state of an open qubit by reshaping its trajectory under Markovian dissipation. A state-error Lyapunov function is adopted to derive an analytical feedback law for Lindblad dynamics, ensuring a nonincreasing Lyapunov function whenever the control sensitivities are nonzero. The analysis identifies the geometric conditions under which the feedback becomes ineffective, showing that control authority vanishes when the current and target Bloch vectors are collinear. Numerical simulations are performed for amplitude damping and pure dephasing using selected target states. Performance is evaluated through fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort. The results demonstrate that the proposed feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but it can provide transient benefits for selected target-channel combinations. In particular, under amplitude damping, the controller significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and substantially extends the interval during which the system remains above a prescribed fidelity threshold. In the pure dephasing cases examined, improvements in fidelity are generally limited, although transient coherence preservation is observed for the oblique target considered, revealing a trade-off between coherence and state fidelity. These findings indicate that Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism and motivate its application to gate operations and preservation of prepared states during finite time intervals before their use or readout.

title: Microwave-optical quantum transduction with quantum-well exciton polaritons
summary: Linking superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber requires microwave-optical quantum transducers that are efficient, high-bandwidth, and low-noise. This combination has been out of reach because of the weak nonlinearities of conventional electro-optic (EO) materials. We propose a transducer with an engineered, strong EO nonlinearity using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons. The QCSE transducer leverages the strong light-matter interactions and extreme polarizability of quantum well excitons. Strong coupling to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical thin-film lithium niobate device. We describe a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer design with predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a $\sim$60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 $μ$W and loaded optical and microwave quality factors of only $3\times10^4$ and $10^3$. We further show that the cavity protection of the polariton provides robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum well excitons.

title: Charge self-consistent DFT+QDMFT framework with a Krylov-based quantum impurity solver
summary: We integrate a quantum impurity solver into a charge self-consistent density functional theory (DFT) plus quantum dynamical mean-field theory framework. The solver optimizes adaptive circuits to approximate the ground state of the impurity model and its particle and hole excitations, and reconstructs the impurity Green's function from their Hamiltonian moments. Higher-order moments are predicted from low-order ones using a machine-learning model, while regularized optimization mitigates violations of causality in the resulting self-energy. The latter is used to update the charge density until self-consistency is achieved. We demonstrate the framework through body-centered cubic lithium calculations and compare the results with a reference one using a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo solver. These calculations converge with root-mean-square charge-density residuals below $\boldsymbol{2\times10^{-3}}$ and yield a nearly vanishing impurity self-energy, consistent with the noninteracting limit used for weakly correlated lithium.

title: Infrared fluctuations and collective entanglement modes in harmonic lattices
summary:
We investigate how infrared fluctuations and spatial separation shape vacuum entanglement between two finite regions in the relativistic harmonic chain and its Lifshitz generalizations. At fixed lattice spacing and finite geometry, we establish that logarithmic negativity remains uniformly bounded as the mass approaches zero, while mutual information diverges. Infrared-enhanced total correlations therefore do not provide an unbounded distillable-entanglement resource. Using local symplectic consolidation, we identify the collective canonical modes carrying the negativity and follow their evolution with separation. Their participation crosses over from localization near the facing boundaries to a collective distribution within each region. Expansion in the adjacent-state canonical basis connects this evolution to progressively weaker, more extended reference modes, including adjacent-halo directions.
  Building on the established concentration of long-distance logarithmic negativity into a single canonical pair, we show that its spatial participation is smooth and infrared-dominated despite its ultraviolet canonical structure, a distinction also present in pure-state entanglement modes. These results refine the ultraviolet mode picture by resolving the long-wavelength organization of the oscillators participating in the surviving entanglement. Across the massless dispersions studied, the normalized participation approaches a universal long-distance profile when separation is scaled by the negativity radius. Its detailed form and the entanglement range nevertheless remain sensitive to ultraviolet deformations. Together, these findings distinguish infrared-enhanced correlations from distillable entanglement and reveal the collective spatial organization underlying its persistence at large separation.

title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
summary: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

title: Quantum Fisher information matrices for time-evolved bosonic Gaussian thermal states
summary: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) is a fundamental quantum metrological quantity arising from the second order term in a Taylor expansion of a smooth divergence evaluated at nearby quantum states. The $α$-$z$ information matrix is a QFI measure arising from the $α$-$z$ Rényi relative entropy, and QFI measures corresponding to various underlying smooth divergences may be recovered from the $α$-$z$ information matrix, including the standard symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) QFI. Bosonic Gaussian states are common probe states for quantum metrological tasks and admit a complete characterization in terms of their first and second moments. In this work, we consider the quantum metrological task of estimating parameters that characterize a Gaussian unitary time evolution of a faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal state. We establish a formula for the $α$-$z$ information matrix of faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states that have undergone a Gaussian unitary time evolution. As an example, we calculate entries of the $α$-$z$ information matrix for a two-mode Gaussian thermal state that has undergone a beam splitting operation. For a parametrized family of time-evolved bosonic Gaussian states, we also derive a formula for the SLD operator, which is known to provide a measurement scheme that saturates the quantum Crámer-Rao bound and thus achieves the ultimate precision for single parameter estimation.

title: A Geometric Framework for Local-to-Global Symmetry: Global Constraints on Local Dynamics
summary: Aggregate molecular systems are routinely understood by decomposing them into local structural units, such as monomers in J/H-aggregates, chemical moieties, motifs, and functional groups. Implicit in such decompositions is the assumption that these local structures remain meaningful within the aggregate. Here, we ask how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry, and how this relation determines the constraints that global symmetry imposes on transitions between local symmetry sectors. We construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and show that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. By identifying which global symmetry sectors overlap each local symmetry sector, we resolve symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Through Frobenius reciprocity, these exclusions can be determined from standard character tables of the local and global symmetry groups, with the character values in the inner product paired according to the relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate. Although motivated by molecular aggregates, the construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.

title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
summary: Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the $\texttt{BP-LSD}$ decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the $\texttt{Beamsearch}$ decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.

title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
summary: The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

title: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval
summary: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.

title: Quantum Information Transfer in Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach
summary: Achieving high-fidelity transfer of an arbitrary quantum state between spatially separated qubits is a central challenge for reliable quantum hardware. We address this question within a polaritonic framework by introducing Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT). Based on quasidegenerate perturbation theory, this approach describes a molecular network coupled to an optical cavity and local phonons through a generalized Holstein--Tavis--Cummings Hamiltonian. Quantum information is encoded in a coherent superposition of exciton-cavity states, while phonons constitute a weakly coupled environment. In the nonadiabatic regime of weak exciton-phonon coupling, the method incorporates phonon-induced renormalization of polaritonic states and their dynamics while reducing the Hamiltonian to independent fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks. This structure provides efficient access to the coherence and population propagators governing quantum-state transfer without invoking a Markovian approximation. We benchmark the approach against exact dynamics for a molecular wheel network, considering both molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer. PB-VVPT accurately reproduces short- and long-time transfer dynamics, including thermal decoherence and fidelity revivals consistent with non-Markovian memory effects, with prediction errors below $1\%$ over most of the simulated time intervals. This accuracy is achieved with an estimated diagonalization cost more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of the exact reference calculations. These results establish PB-VVPT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach to quantum information transfer in molecular polaritonic networks.

title: An alternate proof of the QMA lower bound for set-size estimation
summary: In the set-size estimation query task, a query algorithm decides whether an $N$-bit input has Hamming weight $\ge B$ or $\le A$ (with $\ge B$ as the yes instances and $\le A$ as the no instances). When $B = 2A$, this is sometimes called approximate counting. The query complexity for this problem with a quantum witness (i.e., $\mathsf{QMA}$ query bounds) was resolved by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler (CCC 2020) and proved using Laurent polynomials. Here we give a morally similar but distinct proof of the lower bound using the polynomial method.

title: Transient Synchronization and Entanglement through Shared Dissipation in Circuit QED
summary: We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap $ξ$ whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.

title: Generalized Schrieffer-Wolff transformation
summary: The Schrieffer-Wolff transformation (SWT) is a cornerstone of effective-Hamiltonian theory. However, the SWT is predominantly used for weak-coupling problems, while a systematic counterpart for strongly coupled regimes remains largely unexplored. A general closed-form SWT generator and a clear physical principle for gauge fixing remain elusive, obscuring the transformation's underlying structure. We introduce the dual SWT to deal with the strong-coupling problems. The generalized SWT (gSWT) is formulated for any Hermitian operator and block partition. We establish the geodesic principle for its canonical gauge. Furthermore, we derive an exact closed-form solution of the gSWT generator at every order as a finite nested-commutator sum whose only input is the active gap set. Both the geometric and algebraic aspects of the SWT physics are revealed. The gSWT framework is illustrated in two quantum many-body models, the collective spin model and the transverse-field Ising model.

title: Magic state cultivation with lattice-surgery escape on superconducting hardware
summary: Magic state cultivation (MSC) is a low-overhead protocol for fault-tolerantly preparing logical magic states. In this work, we implement two MSC variants to prepare a magic state in a distance-5 code on a publicly available IBM Nighthawk processor. The first is a lattice-surgery escape, recently proposed by Hirano et al. and experimentally studied here for the first time. The second is a grafting escape, previously demonstrated by Rosenfeld et al., and extended here by incorporating a switch into a matchable code. Both protocols begin with fault-tolerant cultivation of a T state on a color code, followed by an escape into a larger code. We decode the results using minimum-weight perfect matching or Tesseract on circuit-level error models calibrated to the hardware noise. Compared with the previous experiment, our cultivated T state achieves a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the T-state injection angle, nearly 10x lower with about 3x the retainment. Moreover, our execution of the grafting escape has a 2x lower logical error rate per stabilizer round at a higher retainment. When comparing the two protocols under identical execution conditions and complementary gap postselection based on decoder confidence, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code preserves a T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds after escape at about 5% retainment. By contrast, matchable-switched grafting drops below 0.95 fidelity at comparable retainment. Furthermore, the lattice-surgery escape reaches a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% with around 11% average shot retainment. These results establish lattice-surgery escape as a practical MSC protocol that benefits from a direct transition into a surface code, and demonstrate the lowest MSC error and the highest surface-code magic-state fidelity reported to date, advancing the experimental realization of fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.

title: Cantor correlations II. Synchronicity and bisynchronicity
summary: We study synchronous and bisynchronous no-signalling correlations, defined over Cantor topological spaces, from the perspectives of both continuous variable quantum information and operator algebra theories. We focus on strategies, satisfying a natural no-signalling condition across the Cantor space levels, called graded, identifying a universal C*-algebra, whose tracial states of different types characterise synchronous correlations of respective types. The universal C*-algebra for bisynchronous graded correlations is shown to coincide with the C*-algebra of a projective limit of free wreath products of quantum permutation groups, introduced by Bhowmick, Goswami and Skalski, and a type description, analogous to the one in the synchronous case, is provided. Extending results in the finite case, we show that bisynchronous graded correlations canonically give rise to factorisable maps on type I factors, defined via Cantor permutation matrices. We examine non-local games over Cantor topological spaces, with inputs/outputs that are finite words of equal length, define corresponding game algebras, and characterise the perfect strategies of the games via the respective game algebras. In the case of the Cantor graph isomorphism game, we provide equivalent descriptions of the existence of perfect strategies of quantum commuting type, in terms of bigalois correspondences, factorisable maps, Cantor permutation intertwiners and game algebra non-triviality. Our results supply a quantum information interpretation of a notion of a quantum isomorphism of locally finite graphs, introduced by Rollier and Vaes, canonically arising from Cantor graphs.

title: Commutator-guided repair and classical-accessibility boundaries for shallow quantum circuits
summary: Trainability does not guarantee low-energy arrival: a shallow quantum circuit can be optimizable yet fail, under fixed depth and evaluation budgets, to reach Hamiltonian-selected states. We introduce a commutator-guided repair for this operational failure mode. Low-order host--Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations, from which a compact completion layer is selected before full reoptimization. Across 189 paired six-qubit trials, unrepaired circuits achieve 0/189 strict successes, a non-deployable per-trial control envelope achieves 109/189, and two predeclared selectors achieve 133/189 and 127/189. The repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS. Under fixed-depth geometric locality, repaired losses and gradients are classically computable, while corresponding ground-state targets admit low-bond-dimension tensor-network approximations through the tested sizes. The method reveals a trainability--arrival--classical-accessibility tradeoff rather than quantum advantage.

title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

title: Two-Qutrit Quantum Battery Charging through Ising Model and Anisotropic XZ Heisenberg Interactions
comment: 16 Pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in AVS Quantum Science
summary: In this paper, we propose a model of a two-qutrit quantum battery composed of two spin-1 systems coupled to an external field via anisotropic Heisenberg interactions. From the Ising model, we derive an exact analytical expression of ergotropy in the parallel-charging case. However, the collective charging process offers an advantage over the parallel one. Moreover, increasing the collective exchange coupling accelerates the evolution of ergotropy and enhances the maximum average power, as measured by global coherence and mutual information. Conversely, the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction primarily acts as a detrimental mechanism, essentially reducing all of these quantities. In the XZ model, the obtained results show that the DM interaction is constructive when it cooperates with the longitudinal anisotropy and when the exchange coupling is sufficiently strong. Therefore, by optimising the maximum reachable ergotropy and maximum average power, we conclude that the Ising model without DM interaction is sufficient to maximise the ergotropy. The anisotropic XZ model allows the DM interaction to be exploited constructively to improve the maximum average power through the joint control of the exchange coupling, longitudinal anisotropy, and chiral interaction.

title: Exceptional-point Sensing with Quantum Advantage
summary: Exceptional-point sensors exploit singular non-Hermitian dynamics to enhance their response to weak perturbations. Recently, however, a no-go result has been established for a gain-loss-balanced dimer coupled to independent, phase-insensitive reservoirs: the exceptional-point susceptibility amplifies the signal and reservoir noise equally, precluding any quantum advantage. Here, we circumvent this limitation by engineering non-Hermitian dynamics in particle-hole Nambu space. A single common reservoir acts on modes forming a quantum-mechanics-free subsystem and generates an enhanced response protected from additional noise. We demonstrate quantum-metrological advantage for weak-signal sensing and static-parameter estimation. A continuous interpolation of the operator basis at fixed exceptional-point drift, with a singular midpoint, reveals how reservoir noise vanishes toward the protected limit. Our results provide a route to exceptional-point sensing with genuine quantum-metrological advantage through reservoir engineering.

title: Quantum Causal Compatibility from Spatiotemporal Correlations
summary: Which quantum causal structures can account for observed spatiotemporal correlations without access to an intervention-complete description of the underlying process? In particular, can such correlations distinguish a temporal chain, a common cause, and a common effect? Here, we address these questions using three-qubit pseudo-density operators constructed from experimentally accessible Pauli correlations. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for pseudo-Markov compatibility with the chain, fork, and collider structures by relaxing complete positivity while preserving the corresponding quantum Markov constraints. Despite their distinct causal mechanisms, all three pseudo-Markov compatibility problems reduce to linear feasibility tests, without requiring full-rank marginal states. We further establish a unified semidefinite-programming approach to physical realizability and quantify the minimum violation of complete positivity through Choi negativity. Using a two-parameter family of pseudo-density operators, we demonstrate that different causal structures admit overlapping yet non-nested sets of correlations. Our results show that quantum causal explanations need not be unique, but experimentally accessible correlations can nevertheless distinguish and exclude candidate causal structures.

title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
summary: Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns $R(\varphi, \fracπ{2})$ gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.

title: Symmetry-selected entanglement death at Floquet resonances of parametrically coupled qubits
summary: Periodic modulation of a qubit--qubit coupling is a standard way to engineer quantum interactions, but a strong modulation also reorganizes the transitions through which the qubits dissipate into a comb of Floquet channels. We study two identical, strongly coupled qubits whose transverse coupling is modulated anharmonically, as by a nonlinear coupler, with each qubit damped by its own reservoir. The modulation raises the ground-state concurrence of the cycle-averaged Hamiltonian from 0.45 to above 0.8, yet the steady-state concurrence stays close to its undriven value except at Floquet resonances selected by symmetry. There it undergoes entanglement death, vanishing at all times in the drive cycle over a finite range of modulation depths. Parity and exchange symmetry split the Floquet spectrum into an even sector, whose branches anticross at multiphoton resonances, and an exactly solvable odd sector, whose branches cross. Every dissipative channel connects the two sectors, so only the even anticrossings cause entanglement death, provided their gap exceeds the damping rate, whereas the nearby odd crossings leave the concurrence unchanged. Comparing time-independent and Floquet master equations, with and without the secular approximation, we show that the basis in which the dissipator is built changes the entanglement by up to 0.2 for an Ohmic bath and 0.5 for a flat one, whereas the secular approximation matters only near anticrossings with gaps comparable to the damping. The basis matters most when the bath has spectral weight at low frequency, where the drive moves dissipative channels through zero frequency. A transverse field that breaks parity lifts the selection rule.

title: Emergence and Persistence of Maximal Atom-Field Entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings model
comment: To be published in Physica Scripta
summary: We investigate the emergence and persistence of maximal entanglement between a two-level atom and a single-mode quantized electromagnetic field inside a cavity, whose dynamics are governed by the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian. Using the von Neumann entropy as a measure of entanglement, we establish a direct connection between entanglement, atomic coherence, and atomic population inversion. This establishment shows that maximal atom-field entanglement is achieved when both the atomic population inversion and the $l_1$-norm of atomic coherence simultaneously vanish. By considering the atom initially in its excited state, we further demonstrate that the persistence of maximal atom-field entanglement strongly depends on the initial state of the field. For field states whose photon-number distributions have no two consecutive occupied photon-number levels, the local atomic coherence remains zero throughout the evolution. Consequently, complete collapse of the atomic population inversion for an extended period leads to persistent maximal atom-field entanglement. In contrast, for other field states, the interaction generates local atomic coherence, resulting in transient maximal entanglement. Our results demonstrate how the choice of the initial field state controls the temporal characteristics of entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings system. The generation and persistence of maximal atom-field entanglement in such systems could be valuable for applications in quantum information processing.

title: CHEQ: A Concurrent Hardware Evaluation Platform for QEC Decoders via Batch-Invariant Circuit-Level Noise Sampling
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. This paper has been accepted for publication in the Proceedings of DATE 2027
summary: Hardware quantum error correction (QEC) decoders require validation of logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations demand extensive sampling, while algorithm-level software evaluation does not directly measure hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models contain many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient. We present CHEQ, an FPGA platform integrating on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control. Its Sampling Units use geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws and exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. A throughput model guides joint selection of the Sampling Unit count, batch size, and decoder count under FPGA resource constraints. Across evaluated conditions, the pooled one-sided 95% upper bound on the weighted root-mean-square relative firing-rate difference from Stim is 0.16%. At a batch size of 4,096, a Sampling Unit uses only 4.8%-11.2% of a Helios decoder's LUTs for code distances 7, 9, 11, and 13. On an AMD VCU118 FPGA at code distance 7 and physical error rate 10^-3, two Sampling Units supply 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots/s, completing 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes without host-side shot generation.

title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
summary: Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
summary: quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

title: Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering for Multi-Time Correlations
summary: In quantum optimal control, gradient methods are often used to optimize functions of a state or propagator at a final time, while experimentally addressable observables and performance metrics may depend on multi-time correlations. We develop QRT-GRAPE, which combines the quantum regression theorem (QRT) with Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) to obtain analytic gradients for objective functions defined by multi-time correlations. The method incorporates the time evolution of an auxiliary operator in QRT into the forward propagation and backward adjoint propagation used in GRAPE. As an application, we consider the trade-off between the photon-emission probability and the conditional Bell-state fidelity in heralded remote entanglement generation among two nonidentical atom--cavity systems. Starting from a flat-top Rabi pulse pair selected by a search over pulse amplitudes and durations, QRT-GRAPE increases the photon-emission probability product from $0.2802$ to $0.3216$ and the conditional Bell-state fidelity from $0.9356$ to $0.9441$.

title: Optimizing interference zeros for finite-pulse transmission in waveguide quantum electrodynamics
summary: A photon pulse occupies a range of frequencies, so suppressing reflection at its carrier need not minimize the error of the transmitted pulse. We study two separated emitters coupled to a common waveguide at several contact points. Interference between the contact paths can make the coupling that drives each emitter quadratic in frequency detuning. With matched propagation and emitter resonances centered on the carrier, the reflected fields cancel once more. Their combined reflection probability is then sixth order at zero loss. Separating each local double zero into two simple zeros can nevertheless improve transmission of a finite pulse. We minimize the leading narrowband error within this common static adjustment, counting reflection, absorption, and distortion of the transmitted mode. For a Gaussian pulse without loss, the minimum is two-fifths of the error for coincident zeros. Independent emitter loss favors a smaller separation because photons entering separate reservoirs do not share the cancellation of the reflected fields. The optimum follows from the pulse spectrum and the relative weight of these two processes. Uniform and Su--Schrieffer--Heeger waveguides realize the mechanism. In the latter, coordinated contact and resonance adjustments also preserve the full ratio of complex transmission amplitudes for opposite incidence directions. Finite-band calculations determine how the benefit changes with bandwidth and contact errors.

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

title: Strong eigenstate thermalization in Singer-cycle Clifford circuits
summary: Eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides a central framework for understanding thermalization in isolated quantum systems. Recently, the infinite-temperature ETH has been established for almost all Floquet eigenstates in linear feedback shift register quantum circuits. Here we introduce brickwork Clifford circuits with $L$ qubits where the induced transformation of Pauli operators is represented by an irreducible symplectic matrix over the finite field $\mathbb F_2$ of the maximal order $2^L+1$, known as a Singer cycle. For these Singer-cycle Clifford circuits, we prove a strong version of ETH: all Floquet eigenstates are thermal at infinite temperature without exceptions. We derive uniform bounds on both diagonal deviations from thermal expectation values and off-diagonal matrix elements of arbitrary observables supported on a fixed number of sites. The results indicate that long-time averages of observables approach the infinite-temperature values in the thermodynamic limit for arbitrary initial states. We also show that the temporal fluctuation of expectation values of observables is exponentially suppressed in the thermodynamic limit, implying that each observable remains close to the infinite-temperature value for almost all times.

title: Optimal Measurement Rounds for Perfect Encoded Fusion
summary: Encoded fusion combines probabilistic physical fusions to perform a logical Bell measurement. Adaptive choices depend on earlier measurement outcomes and therefore require multiple measurement rounds. We determine the minimum worst-case number of rounds for perfect fusion of two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code. A strategy is perfect if the logical Bell measurement succeeds on every branch containing at least one successful physical fusion. Even after fixing the past history, including measurement values, we consider all success/failure branches, including those with zero probability for a particular input state or measurement device. In a lossless model with fixed coordinate pairing, arbitrary Pauli failure bases, and each pair fused exactly once, the optimum equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code. The lower bound applies to arbitrary perfect strategies that choose batches and bases using previous outcomes. We also characterize the batch sequences that can occur on an all-failure branch of a perfect strategy by a necessary and sufficient graph adjacency condition. A matching strategy fuses distance layers from the outside in and, after the first success, completes the remaining fusions in at most one further round by changing the failure bases along an induced path.

title: Generating Massive Mechanical Superpositions through Qubit-Mediated Interference
summary: We propose a method towards demonstrating a quantum superposition of a massive mechanical resonator without the need for exact ground-state cooling, a requirement that becomes increasingly difficult to satisfy for low-frequency resonators. Our scheme relies on coupling the resonator to a spin-qubit. Using magnetic force coupling between the motion of the mechanical resonator and the spin-qubit, the resonator is forced into attracted and repelled states as the spin-qubit is coherently controlled. Interference between the resonator states can be observed when a series of $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses is applied to the spin-qubit within the coherence time of the resonator. The protocol describes a true which-path interference experiment suitable for use at ultra-low temperatures, since it requires only three $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses, separated in time by half a mechanical period, thus minimizing the heat-load and duration of the experiment. By analysing the experimental requirements necessary to successfully execute the protocol, we show that the protocol is suitable for resonators in a broad regime of resonance frequencies, ranging from 1kHz resonators, which have the advantage of a relatively high spin-coupling, to resonators of more than 100kHz, whose mechanical mode is easier to cool. We show that interference remains visible for resonator mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons. Lastly, we observe that an implementation of the protocol with low-frequency mechanical resonators provides a promising approach towards testing objective collapse models.

title: Analytical prediction of superradiant burst dynamics in extended atomic ensembles
summary: We present an open-system quantum theory of forward superradiant bursts in extended two-level atomic ensembles using coupled Heisenberg-Langevin and Maxwell propagation equations. Starting from a fully inverted state with zero mean polarization, local dipole correlations initiate emission without a prescribed tipping angle or stochastic seed. Assuming a spatially uniform population inversion while retaining longitudinal field propagation and spatially dependent atomic polarization, we derive an analytical expression for the absolute photon emission rate into the selected forward optical channel. Coupled to self-consistent inversion dynamics, the expression quantitatively reproduces the pulse waveform and absolute peak rate from spatially resolved stochastic simulations for the sample parameters considered, up to an optical depth (OD) of approximately 200.
